title: Rate Limiting
summary: Protect shared capacity by deciding who may do how much, and what happens when they ask for more.
keyPoints: Rate limiting protects capacity, fairness, and cost rather than blocking all traffic.
Token bucket allows bursts up to a bucket size while enforcing an average rate.
Fixed windows are simple but allow a burst at the boundary; sliding windows smooth it.
Distributed counters need an atomic increment or a small amount of over-admission.
Return 429 with Retry-After and make limits visible in headers.
commonMistakes: Using a fixed window and allowing twice the intended rate at the boundary.
Storing a counter per node, so the effective limit is multiplied by the number of nodes.
Rejecting requests without a Retry-After or a clear error body.
Rate-limiting by IP only when users share NAT or proxies.
interviewNotes: Ask whether the limit is per user, per IP, per API key, or per tenant.
State the burst allowance separately from the average rate.
Explain where the counter lives and what happens if it is unavailable.
Decide whether the limiter fails open or closed during a store outage.

checkYourself.question: How does a token bucket allow a short burst?
checkYourself.answer: Tokens accumulate up to a bucket size. A burst can spend the stored tokens, while the refill rate enforces the long-term average.

checkYourself.question: Why is a fixed window boundary a problem?
checkYourself.answer: A client can send the full quota at the end of one window and again at the start of the next, producing twice the intended rate in a short span.

checkYourself.question: What should the server return when a limit is exceeded?
checkYourself.answer: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, with Retry-After and useful rate-limit headers so the client can back off correctly.
